cards.title: Diagnose Google Ads health in the right order
cards.summary: Use a fixed sequence of account-level metrics to find the real bottleneck before touching campaigns.
cards.use_when: Your Google Ads spend is rising but profit is flat, and you need to decide whether to fix creative, landing page, offer or campaign setup before scaling budget.
steps: Pull six metrics: impression share, average CPC, CTR, conversion rate, number of conversions, and average session duration.
Read them in that priority order — the source treats impression share as the leading indicator: low impression share predicts high CPC, low CTR, low conversion rate and few conversions.
Treat average session duration as the congruence check between ad promise and landing page; short sessions suggest the ad and page are saying different things.
Only after those site/offer-level numbers look sound, move to Google Ads mechanics (conversion tracking, structure, creative, bids).
Interpret the benchmark contextually: lower impression share means competitors are outbidding or out-converting you, which is a spend/offer problem, not just a bidding problem.
caveats: The source asserts impression share is the single most important metric for ecommerce; this is a practitioner heuristic, not a Google-documented rule.
Session duration is the source's informal ad-to-page congruence proxy, not a formal diagnostic metric.

cards.title: Set up Shopify-to-Google Ads purchase conversion tracking
cards.summary: Configure enhanced conversions with purchase as the primary goal, then correctly order the remaining funnel events.
cards.use_when: You are launching Google Ads or your reported conversions do not match Shopify orders and you need trustworthy purchase data before scaling.
steps: Install Google Analytics 4 via the Shopify Google & YouTube app first, then in Google Ads go to Goals > Settings and switch on enhanced conversions using the Google tag method.
In Goals > Conversions > Summary, create new conversion actions for purchase, add to cart, begin checkout and product view (page view).

For the purchase action: add to account-default goals, mark as primary, use different values per conversion, count every conversion, and set click-through window to 90 days and engage-view and view-through windows to 30 days.
Set attribution to data-driven and manage conversions through the Google tag.
Import the prebuilt Google Tag Manager container, then paste the conversion ID and each of the four conversion labels into the matching GTM constants and publish the workspace.
In Shopify admin > Settings > Customer Events, add a custom pixel, paste the GTM customer-event code, set your country code and insert your GTM container ID, then save and connect.
Finally, edit add to cart, begin checkout and product view to Secondary (observe only) so they do not drive bidding; keep purchase as the account default goal.
caveats: The exact menu paths and prebuilt container are from the source's 2025 workflow; verify current Google Ads and Shopify interfaces before following step by step.
Turning non-purchase events to secondary assumes purchase is your optimisation event — different goals may justify a different primary.

cards.title: Structure campaigns by funnel stage and start at the bottom
cards.summary: Split cold, mid-funnel and branded campaigns so cold and branded conversion data stay visible and separately attributable.
cards.use_when: You are planning a Google Ads account architecture or reworking an account where branded and non-branded results are blended and unreadable.
steps: Top of funnel: YouTube Shorts and static assets run through Demand Gen, fed by your Meta winners at roughly $50/day, running fully broad with the creative doing the targeting.
Mid funnel: cold search, competitive search (only if it works well), Performance Max and cold Shopping.
Bottom funnel: branded search, branded shopping and dynamic remarketing.

If you are just starting, begin at the bottom of the funnel to accumulate conversions, then add one mid-funnel campaign — for ecommerce usually Shopping and PMax — and only move up-funnel once smart bidding is viable.
Exclude all customer lists from cold campaigns and exclude your brand from PMax so branded conversions do not inflate cold performance.
Keep branded search and branded shopping in separate campaigns so cheap branded conversions stay identifiable and marketing spend stays efficient.
caveats: The source's rule of thumb for smart bidding eligibility is about one conversion per day sustained over 30 days — treat as a heuristic, not a Google requirement.
Running your Meta winners as YouTube statics/shorts is a transfer assumption; test rather than assuming parity.

cards.title: Write Google ads from audience research, not keyword lists
cards.summary: Ground search ads, shopping titles and YouTube angles in the language and motivations of the person searching.
cards.use_when: You are writing search ad copy, shopping titles or a YouTube short for a cold audience and need angle and language direction.
steps: Before writing anything, map the audience: the language they use, psychographics, problems, pains, goals, desires, why they buy and why they buy from you specifically.
Ask explicitly: what type of person searches this, what pain are they in, what problem are they solving, what desire or goal does the product fulfil.
Write search headlines, descriptions, images, callouts, site links and snippets that echo that language, since on Google the searcher is seeing every competitor's ad simultaneously.
In shopping ads, carry the same language into the title (for targeting) plus the promo extension, ratings and social proof that visually differentiate the listing.

For YouTube Shorts use heavy direct response: make the CTA explicit (click here, search this, tap the screen) and state the big offer and next step, because the platform is less purchase-oriented than Meta.
The source argues resonance, connection and offer are what make you stand out — not just being cheapest, since margin constrains price competition.
caveats: The claim that cheap price would win all else being equal is the source's framing; margin reality often prevents it.
Heavy-direct-response guidance is the source's opinion about YouTube's buying sophistication, not a measured universal rule.

cards.title: Let Shopping and PMax discover your converting keywords
cards.summary: Use broad-match Shopping/PMax search term reports as first-party keyword research rather than guessing keywords upfront.
cards.use_when: You need real, purchase-confirmed search phrases for search campaigns, shopping titles or landing page copy.
steps: Launch Shopping and PMax broadly and let Google test a wide range of search terms automatically rather than pre-selecting keywords.
Read the search term report inside Google Ads and rank queries by impressions, CTR, conversions and CPC.
In Shopping, this also reveals what your product title is actually matching against, which tells you what your feed title is communicating.
Extract converting queries into exact and phrase match keywords in search campaigns — start with exact for proven winners, phrase for close variations.
Push the same winning phrases into product titles, PMax assets, YouTube angles, offers and landing page copy.
Exclude the low-performing and non-converting search terms to raise efficiency, then repeat: the loop is a flywheel, not a one-time task.
Example: a shopping feed surfaces 'best marathon shoes for flat feet' as converting, so you'd otherwise never have intuited that query and can now target it exactly and build copy around it.
caveats: This inverts traditional keyword-first research; the source recommends manual keyword research only for your very first search campaigns or when you need control.
The source claims broad will not work in search campaigns unless you are explicitly testing — validate data elsewhere first.

cards.title: Use manual keyword tools only for the first rung
cards.summary: Seed initial search campaigns with third-party keyword data, then hand research over to Google's conversion data.
cards.use_when: You have no conversion history and must launch a first search campaign or decide initial product title targets.
steps: Use Google Keyword Planner on your main product category to find general product-level search phrases with high search volume and reasonable CPCs.
Use paid tools (Ahrefs, Semrush) to reverse-engineer competitor keywords, and SpyFu to see what competitors are bidding on.
Treat competitor bidding as weak evidence: the source says assume competitors may be bidding on terms that do not work for them.
Note the limitation: third-party data gives search volume and competitor behaviour but no purchase confirmation for your product.
Use these keywords only to seed, then let Shopping/PMax conversion data replace and refine them over time.
Best combined approach per the source: start broad with method one (let Google optimise for speed and scale), then layer traditional research for extra optimisation.
caveats: High search volume without buyer intent is a poor target; the source stresses buy intent over volume.
Keyword Planner and third-party tool interfaces change frequently — verify current functionality.

cards.title: Set bids and budgets from unit economics, not habit
cards.summary: Choose bidding strategies per campaign type and let your margins and KPIs define how much you can afford to bid and spend.
cards.use_when: You are setting bid strategy and daily budget for branded, shopping, PMax or cold campaigns.
steps: Work backwards from unit economics: how much can you afford to spend per acquisition to beat competitors, and how much are you willing to spend to test versus scale.
Match strategy to campaign type: branded search runs on target impression share (the source calls it absolute target impression share); branded shopping runs on manual CPC where you control max CPC.
Mid-funnel and cold campaigns use smart bidding: maximise conversion value for ecommerce (more value per purchase), maximise conversions when you want volume, plus tROAS and tCPA variants.
Choose maximise conversions over value only when you know your break-even CPA and simply want as many actions as possible; otherwise value-based bidding is the ecommerce default per the source.
The source treats bids and budget as the last optimisation area — after creative, structure, tracking and offer — though it still matters.
Budget levels depend entirely on brand specifics: goals, KPIs, COGS and desired scale; there is no universal number.
caveats: The source explicitly gives a non-specific answer on budget size because it depends on individual brand economics — do not copy another brand's budget.
Smart bidding requires sufficient conversion volume to learn; bid strategy names and settings change, so verify in the current Google Ads interface.

cards.title: Enrol the four GMC add-ons
cards.summary: Turn on dynamic remarketing, customer reviews, product ratings and promotions in Merchant Center to lift CTR and enable remarketing.
cards.use_when: You are setting up or auditing Google Merchant Center before running Shopping, PMax or remarketing.
steps: Go to Merchant Center Settings > Add-ons and check the Discover tab for programs you are not enrolled in.
Enable dynamic remarketing — the source says it is essential for the whole Google Ads system to function for ecommerce.
Enable Google customer reviews and product ratings to add trust signals that the source claims noticeably raise CTR and conversion rate on ads.
Enable promotions so your discount appears in the Shopping ad itself; the source argues a visible better offer wins the click and increases purchase likelihood.
Verify each add-on is actually active, not just available, before spending on feed campaigns.
caveats: CTR and conversion-rate lifts from reviews/ratings/promotions are stated by the source without specific measured figures — treat as directional.
Eligibility for some add-ons varies by country and account standing.

cards.title: Complete GMC business info and branding to survive review
cards.summary: Fill business details, verified store, logo/colour assets and social profiles accurately to protect account standing.
cards.use_when: You are onboarding a store to Merchant Center or your account has warnings and you want to reduce suspension risk.
steps: In Business Info, enter details that exactly match your website: verify and claim your online store, provide your checkout link, accepted payment methods, and business logo and colours.
In the same screen use Edit logo and colours to upload square and rectangular logos plus a main and accent colour, so Shopping ads look on-brand and Google sees a complete, legitimate business.
Verify your website branding, payment methods and policies are genuinely consistent with what you enter — the source warns Google is ruthless about mismatches that lead to account suspension.
If in the US, enable business identity attributes: category options include woman-owned, veteran-owned, black-owned, Latino-owned and small business.
The source recommends selecting small business even for larger companies, citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics threshold of under $40 million annual revenue as qualifying as small.
Add social profiles (Instagram, Facebook and others) to make business information as complete as possible.
caveats: The small-business threshold is the source's interpretation of Bureau of Labor Statistics classification, not a Google eligibility rule — verify current Google criteria.
Identity attributes are flagged as a minor CTR/social-standing factor, not a major performance lever.

cards.title: Lock shipping and returns as manual in GMC
cards.summary: Fix shipping and returns configuration inside Merchant Center so Shopify changes cannot desync policies and trigger suspension.
cards.use_when: You are configuring Merchant Center shipping/returns or your store changes shipping rates and you fear feed or policy mismatches.
steps: In the Shopify Google & YouTube sales channel, under product feed settings, set shipping settings to Manual setup in GMC so changes in Shopify do not auto-update Merchant Center.
The source's reasoning: a random sync change can create a mismatch with your stated shipping policy and a flag can escalate to account suspension.
In Merchant Center > Shipping and returns, add policies for every country you ship to, including differing speeds and methods (the example brand runs both US and Canada).
Enter an accurate ship-from location.
Add your returns policy inside GMC, link directly to the specific returns policy page, and ensure it mirrors what is on your site.
Treat a clear, strong return policy as effectively a requirement to run Merchant Center today, and as something Google checks when deciding to suspend.
caveats: Keeping settings manual means you must update GMC yourself when shipping genuinely changes — do it as part of the routine maintenance cycle.
Google's policy and feeds interfaces change; verify that manual-mode options still exist before relying on the workflow.

cards.title: Audit feeds and fix 'needs attention' errors
cards.summary: Locate your primary feed and systematically clear product-level errors before scaling feed ads.
cards.use_when: You are diagnosing why feed ads underperform, or onboarding a store whose products are disapproved or warning-flagged.
steps: In Merchant Center settings, open Data sources to see every feed; with the Shopify Google & YouTube app the primary feed comes via the content API.
Identify your primary feed and any supplemental feeds, confirm the primary is updating, and note that promotions sources can also live here.
Go to Products > Needs attention to see Google's per-SKU issues; the example shows approved products missing an age group.
Work through the list systematically, fixing red errors and yellow warnings using Google's own stated fix instructions.
Make this a weekly routine: revisit Products and diagnostics each week and clear new red or yellow flags before they accumulate.
caveats: The source notes many brands never do this and blame Google Ads for what is a feed problem — expect meaningful time cost with large SKU counts.
Some errors only apply to specific categories (e.g. age group for certain verticals), so not every flag is relevant to every product.

cards.title: Build product titles with the 130–150 character formula
cards.summary: Frontload high-volume keywords and differentiators in feed titles, placing brand first or last depending on brand strength.
cards.use_when: You are rewriting Shopping/PMax feed titles to raise relevance and win more qualifying impressions.
steps: Write titles of roughly 130–150 characters including: highest-volume keyword, product details (colour, size, quantity), second highest-volume keyword, differentiating angles/USPs, and brand name.
For a small brand pushing cold traffic, frontload the high-volume keywords and place the brand name at the end.
For a big brand that can leverage recognition in Shopping, place the brand name first and the high-volume keywords after.
Cover variant fields — colour, size, weight, format — so searchers know exactly what they are buying.
Apply the difference between high-volume keyword (the most product-aware term everyone uses), variants, USPs/angles and brand name in that structure.
Edit titles in Merchant Center > Products by opening the SKU and using Edit product, or manage them in a data feed tool like DataFeedWatch.
You can paste the formula and your product info into ChatGPT to generate a draft, then edit the keyword choices yourself.
caveats: The 130–150 character target is the source's recommendation; verify current Google title length limits before publishing.
The example 'Apple Watch band' title shows the pattern but is a case illustration, not a performance promise.

cards.title: Write feed descriptions that survive policy review
cards.summary: Use the description for targeting and benefit copy, not promotions, and avoid website copy dumps.
cards.use_when: You are optimising feed descriptions for a store that simply imports Shopify product copy into Merchant Center.
steps: Check your current description: if it is auto-pulled from the Shopify product page, assume it is not optimised for feed targeting.
Write roughly 1,000 characters covering key features, USPs, a call to action and useful product information.
Frontload high-volume keywords at the start, in the style of an SEO article, because Google uses the description for targeting.
Exclude promotional text such as discount claims, because the source states that violates Google's policies.
Treat description as secondary in impact to the title, but still worth the effort because it expands the terms your product can match against.
caveats: The source calls the description less leveraged than the title — prioritise titles first.
Promotion language belongs in Merchant Center promotions, not the description; policy details can change, so verify current rules.

cards.title: Choose feed images for context and standout
cards.summary: Test main images that show the product in use versus on plain backgrounds to improve Shopping ad click appeal.
cards.use_when: You are choosing or testing primary feed images for product pages and Shopping/PMax assets.
steps: Select the highest quality, most attention-grabbing image available for each SKU as the primary feed image.

Test the product alone on a clean background against the product in context: a sofa in a well-lit living room setup, golf clubs mid-swing on the green, an Apple Watch band shown on an actual Apple Watch.
Show a product in the context it was made for when the item alone is confusing — the Apple Watch band only makes sense attached to a watch.
Supplement with lifestyle images of people using the product for other placements.
For this source's example brand, the product-focused image performed best; treat that as their finding and run your own test rather than copying it.
caveats: The source is explicit that the best-performing image style is brand-specific — do not assume product-only wins for your category.
Main image choice can affect eligibility and performance simultaneously; check policy requirements alongside conversion appeal.

cards.title: Fill product identifiers, categories and attributes accurately
cards.summary: Use GTINs, product type, category and filtering attributes to remove performance-limiting warnings and increase discoverability.
cards.use_when: Your feed shows warnings about identifiers or missing attributes, or you want products to appear under Shopping filters.
steps: Never change the product ID or SKU; let them import consistently from Shopify or a feed tool, because changing them disrupts history and targeting.
Provide GTIN, UPC, EAN, JAN or ISBN if your product has one — ask your supplier and register the barcode in the feed; custom-made products may legitimately lack one.
Set product type and Google product category for every SKU (the source suggests asking ChatGPT for a first draft), condition to new unless genuinely used, plus accurate price and availability.

Complete detailed attributes used in Shopping filters: colour, size, size type, sizing system by country, gender, material, pattern, age group for apparel; bundle status, adult and energy class where relevant.
Leave shipping and returns to pull from Shopify or the policies configured in GMC.
Add custom labels (e.g. label 1 for small bands, label 2 for large bands) so you can target and report on cohorts inside Google Ads.
Keep COGS, sell quantity and currency fields filled where applicable, though the source calls these minor for performance.
caveats: Missing correct identifiers create performance-limiting warnings rather than outright ban in most cases — still fix them early.
Attribute requirements and identifier rules vary by category and country; check current Merchant Center requirements.

cards.title: Never edit price or availability inside GMC
cards.summary: Change price, availability and sale price only at source so Google does not flag a website mismatch.
cards.use_when: You are updating product pricing or stock and deciding where to make the change.
steps: Make all price, availability and sale price changes in Shopify (or your store platform), never directly in Merchant Center.
Let the change flow back into GMC through the feed so the value matches what a shopper sees on your site.
Understand the risk: Merchant Center checks for mismatches between the site price and the feed price, flags a warning, and repeated mismatches compound account risk.
Treat this as part of weekly and monthly maintenance: review feed values against the live site during routine checks.
If a value genuinely must change in GMC for a feed-only reason, confirm the source-of-truth logic first so the next sync does not overwrite or re-flag it.
caveats: The rule applies to price, availability and sale price specifically; other attributes such as titles and descriptions are edited in the feed.
This is the source's stated best practice for avoiding suspension — enforcement behaviour can change, so keep site and feed aligned regardless.

cards.title: Earn the Shopping experience scorecard badge
cards.summary: Use Google's store quality scorecard to catch missing trust factors and differentiate listings with a trusted badge.
cards.use_when: You want Shopping listings to stand out against competitors and are looking for the highest-leverage remaining trust improvements.
steps: Open the Shopping experience scorecard in Merchant Center and read which components are missing or underperforming.
Work through the components it covers: shipping experience, return experience, purchase experience, browsing experience and promotion data.
Use the edit links to correct shipping details, returns information, purchase experience and browsing experience directly.
Aim to reach the exceptional tier, which the source says earns a trusted badge on Shopping listings and is measured comparatively against competitors.
Combine this with active product ratings and promotions (see the add-ons card) since they feed the same trust layer.
The source's own example sits at number one in its industry for this scorecard, which they attribute to a well-optimised Merchant Center — treat as their result, not a guarantee.
caveats: The badge is awarded comparatively against competitors in your industry, so you can improve and still not hold it.
Scorecard components and point thresholds change; check the current scorecard requirements.

cards.title: Run a weekly and monthly GMC maintenance rhythm
cards.summary: Keep Merchant Center healthy with recurring checks for feed errors, policy drift and promotion dates.
cards.use_when: You run feed campaigns continuously and need an operating routine that prevents gradual account decay or suspension.
steps: Weekly: go through Products and diagnostics, fixing any new red errors and yellow warnings.
Monthly: briefly review your website shipping and returns policies against what is configured in Merchant Center and correct any drift.
When a new sale or promotion starts, add it to GMC promotions and set a proper end date; when the sale ends, make sure the promotion expires or is removed.
Keep the go-to-market discipline of never editing price, availability or sale price in GMC, so maintenance stays focused on feed hygiene rather than correcting mismatches.
Treat this as the ongoing layer on top of the one-time setup phases: account and business setup, shipping/returns/tax, feed health, and trust/visibility.
caveats: The source frames nine out of ten brands as not having Merchant Center set up correctly — expect setup debt, not just ongoing tweaks.
Promotion scheduling mistakes can leave stale offers live, so calendar the end dates.

cards.title: Reduce Merchant Center suspension risk deliberately
cards.summary: Treat suspension as the highest-cost ecommerce event and run the checklist that keeps feed, Shopping and PMax running.
cards.use_when: You are auditing an account for suspension risk or your store has received warnings, mismatches or policy flags.
steps: Prioritise the most common triggers the source identifies: inaccurate business information, mismatched shipping and returns policies, and price/availability mismatches between site and feed.
Keep business info, checkout link, payment methods and branding accurate and consistent with the live site at all times.
Set shipping settings to manual in GMC and maintain policies per country with an accurate ship-from location.
Link directly to a real returns policy page and mirror the policy in Greenhouse Center configuration.
Clear feed errors and warnings weekly rather than letting them stack, and never edit price, availability or sale price inside GMC.
Recognise the stakes: a ban blocks feed ads, Shopping ads, and the strongest part of PMax for an ecommerce brand, so prevention work outranks other optimisation.
caveats: This is a prevention checklist, not an appeals process — a suspended account needs its own remediation path.
Google's policy enforcement and specific triggers are opaque and change; treat the list as risk reduction rather than a guarantee.
